title: Post earnings: the gap and the drift
teaches: Read the day after earnings: what an earnings gap is, a Power Earnings Gap versus a gap that fades, why the close and the volume matter, where to risk against on day one, and the post-earnings drift as a measured but shrinking tendency, never a promise.

facts.quote: Companies may announce important news or financial information outside of regular trading hours.
facts.claim: Companies may release important news and financial results outside the regular session.

facts.quote: These announcements, combined with other extended-hours trading risks, may lead to significant price changes in these companies’ stocks during extended hours trading.
facts.claim: That news can move a stock sharply before or after the regular session.

facts.quote: The prices of some stocks traded during extended-hours trading may not reflect the prices of those stocks during regular hours, either at the end of the regular trading session or upon the opening of regular trading the next business day.
facts.claim: An after-hours price may not match the price at the next regular open.

facts.quote: The reduced level of trading interest in extended-hours trading generally results in wider spreads between the bid and ask prices for a stock or no quotes at all.
facts.claim: After-hours trading is thin: wider spreads, sometimes no quote at all.

facts.quote: if markets are volatile and stock prices are changing rapidly, your stop order may be executed at a price that’s significantly different from your stop price.
facts.claim: In a fast market, a stop can fill far from its stop price.

facts.quote: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached. The price you receive upon execution, though, could be markedly different than your stop price.
facts.claim: A triggered stop becomes a market order, and the fill can be well away from the stop price.

facts.quote: Rapid price movement during a short period of time could trigger a stop order. Due to market volatility, the stock might later rebound and resume trading at its prior price level.
facts.claim: A quick, sharp dip can trigger a stop, and the stock can then bounce right back.

facts.quote: Price charts often have blank spaces known as gaps, representing times when no shares were traded within a particular price range.
facts.claim: A gap is a blank space on the chart: a price range where no shares traded.

facts.quote: For an up gap to form, the low price after the market closes must be higher than the high price of the previous day.
facts.claim: An up gap forms when the day's low stays above the previous day's high.

facts.quote: For example, if an unexpectedly strong earnings report comes out after the market has closed, a lot of buying interest will be generated overnight. This results in an imbalance between supply and demand.
facts.claim: A strong report after the close builds buying interest overnight, so demand outweighs supply at the next open.

facts.quote: If the stock price remains above the previous day's high throughout the day, then an up gap is formed.
facts.claim: The up gap only stands if price stays above the previous day's high all day.

facts.quote: Up and down gaps can form on daily, weekly, or monthly charts and are considered significant when accompanied by above average volume.
facts.claim: Gaps count as significant when volume is above average.

facts.quote: Prices often gap up or down at market open, but the gap does not last until the market closes. Such temporary intraday gaps should not be considered as having any more significance than normal market volatility.
facts.claim: A gap that does not last to the close means no more than normal volatility.

facts.quote: “Getting filled” means that the price action at a later time (a few days to a few weeks) usually retraces, at the least, to the last day before the gap.
facts.claim: A gap is filled when price later comes back to the last day before the gap.

facts.quote: Breakaway gaps are exciting. These occur when the price action is breaking out of a trading range or congestion area.
facts.claim: A breakaway gap breaks price out of a trading range.

facts.quote: Avoid falling into the trap of thinking this type of gap, if associated with good volume, will be filled soon. It might take a long time for the gap to be filled.
facts.claim: A breakaway gap on good volume may not fill for a long time.

facts.quote: Exhaustion gaps happen near the end of a good up or downtrend. The gaps are often the first signal of the end of that move.
facts.claim: Exhaustion gaps come near the end of a long trend and often mark its end.

facts.quote: They're identified by high volume and a large price difference between the previous day's close and the new opening price. They can easily be mistaken for runaway gaps if you overlook the exceptionally high volume.
facts.claim: Exhaustion gaps come on high volume and are easy to mistake for runaway (continuation) gaps.

facts.quote: Waiting for breakout or runaway gaps to be filled can devastate your portfolio. Similarly, waiting for prices to fill a gap before getting on board a trend might make you miss a big move.
facts.claim: Waiting for a strong gap to fill before buying can mean missing the move.

facts.quote: A gap is a change in price levels between the close and open of two consecutive days.
facts.claim: A gap is measured from one day's close to the next day's open.

facts.quote: those labels are applied after the chart pattern is established. That is, the difference between any one type of gap from another is only distinguishable after the stock continues up or down in some fashion.
facts.claim: Gap types (breakaway, exhaustion and so on) can only be told apart after the stock has moved on.

facts.quote: If the stock gaps up, but there is insufficient buying pressure to sustain the rise, the stock price will level or drop below the opening gap price.
facts.claim: Without enough buying, a gap up stalls or falls below its opening price.

facts.quote: The basic tenet of gap trading is to allow one hour after the market opens for the stock price to establish its range.
facts.claim: StockCharts' gap method waits an hour after the open for the range to form.

facts.quote: if ABC company closed yesterday at 10.00 and opened today at 11.00, "filling the gap" would occur when ABC fell back to 10.00.
facts.claim: Filling a gap up means falling back to the prior close.

facts.quote: For me, it's not about THE GAP. It's about WHY did it gap and what happens AFTER the gap?
facts.claim: What matters is why the stock gapped and how it trades after the gap.

facts.quote: Those hollow candles mean that VDSI was closing near its high of the day. In other words, there wasn't just an imbalance of demand at the open that later subsided.
facts.claim: Closing near the high shows demand did not just flare at the open and fade.

facts.quote: The demand continued throughout the day with buyers swarming right up until the closing bell.
facts.claim: A close near the high means buyers kept coming all session.

facts.quote: Well, we never know for sure and that's why we always keep our stops in place - to limit our downside.
facts.claim: Nobody knows which earnings gap will work, so the stop stays in place.

facts.quote: Gaps occur when today's high is below yesterday's low (bearish gap), or today's low is above yesterday's high (bullish gap).
facts.claim: A bullish gap is a day whose low is above the prior day's high.

facts.quote: Gaps are useful for showing support or resistance zones but as a tradeable, by the time you properly identify them, the move is nearly over.
facts.claim: By the time you can properly name a gap's type, the move is nearly over.

facts.quote: Starts a new trend and the gap often occurs on leaving a consolidation area, usually on high volume on the gap day, which can continue for several days.
facts.claim: A breakaway gap leaves a consolidation area, usually on high volume, and starts a trend.

facts.quote: Happens at the end of a trend on high volume. The gap is usually not followed by new highs or lows, and the gap may be unusually tall.
facts.claim: An exhaustion gap comes at the end of a trend on high volume, is often unusually tall, and new highs do not follow.

facts.quote: Look for a high volume gap and trade in the direction of the trend. The best performance comes from breakaway gaps in a bull market near the yearly high.
facts.claim: Breakaway gaps did best in a bull market near the yearly high.

facts.quote: Exhaustion gaps usually close within a week.
facts.claim: Exhaustion gaps usually fill within a week.

facts.quote: Gaps in an uptrend (rising windows) show underlying support 20% of the time in a bull market and 16% of the time in a bear market.
facts.claim: Up gaps acted as support only 20% of the time in a bull market (16% in a bear market).

facts.quote: Often very tall gaps will be exhaustion gaps. That makes sense because traders want to take profits after a large gap, which causes price to reverse and fill the gap or attempt to do so.
facts.claim: Very tall gaps are often exhaustion gaps, because traders take profits after a big jump.

facts.quote: A good earnings surprise is an event pattern in which a company issues an earnings announcement and the market interprets it as better than expected.
facts.claim: A good earnings surprise is a report the market reads as better than expected.

facts.quote: The company announces earnings and the stock makes a large upward move that day or the next if the market was closed.
facts.claim: The big move comes on report day, or the next session if the report came while the market was closed.

facts.quote: Look for announcements in which price makes a large intraday price swing, 2 or 3 times the average daily intraday price range over the last month.
facts.claim: Earnings days with the best setups swing 2 or 3 times the normal daily range.

facts.quote: Select patterns with heavy announcement day volume, above the 30-day average.
facts.claim: Bulkowski wants report-day volume above the 30-day average.

facts.quote: Wait for price to confirm the pattern because traders may push price down instead. An upward breakout (confirmation) happens when price closes above the high posted on the announcement day
facts.claim: Bulkowski waits for a close above the report-day high, because sellers may push the stock down instead.

facts.quote: Failure rates are high. Almost half (48%) rise just 10% before tumbling and that occurs in less than 2 weeks.
facts.claim: Almost half of good earnings surprises rose just 10% and then tumbled, inside 2 weeks.

facts.quote: Trade with the trend. Buy an upward breakout only if the market and industry are trending higher.
facts.claim: Bulkowski buys only when the market and the industry trend up.

facts.quote: Volume on the day price gaps higher must be at least 1.5 times the 50-day average.
facts.claim: In Bulkowski's reading of their rules, Kacher and Morales want gap-day volume at least 1.5 times the 50-day average.

facts.quote: Sell if price closes below the low posted on the day price gaps up.
facts.claim: In Bulkowski's reading of their rules, Kacher and Morales sell on a close below the gap day's low.

facts.quote: I don't like that you're losing two out of every three trades
facts.claim: In Bulkowski's test of their gap-up rules, about two trades in three lost.

facts.quote: A breakaway gap occurs when the price gaps above resistance or gaps below support.
facts.claim: A breakaway gap jumps through resistance (or support).

facts.quote: A breakaway gap with larger than average volume, or especially high volume, shows strong conviction in the gap direction.
facts.claim: Above-average volume on a breakaway gap shows conviction.

facts.quote: If the volume is low on a breakaway gap there is a greater chance of failure.
facts.claim: A breakaway gap on low volume is more likely to fail.

facts.quote: A failed breakout occurs when the price gaps above resistance or below support but can't sustain the price and moves back into the prior trading range.
facts.claim: A failed gap breakout falls back into the old range.

facts.quote: Gaps can occur at any time but are highly likely to occur following earnings announcements or other major corporate announcements.
facts.claim: Gaps are highly likely after earnings and other big company news.

facts.quote: Since an exhaustion gap usually occurs near the end of the trend, any progress the gap made is usually erased (gap filled) within a few weeks and often within several days.
facts.claim: Exhaustion gaps come near a trend's end and usually fill within weeks, often within days.

facts.quote: A gap is filled when the price returns to its pre-gap level.
facts.claim: A gap is filled when price returns to where it was before the gap.

facts.quote: It’s referred to as fading when gaps are filled within the same trading day on which they occur.
facts.claim: A gap that fills on the same day it happens is called fading.

facts.quote: A stock may gap up the next day if the company’s earnings exceed expectations.
facts.claim: Earnings that beat expectations can gap a stock up the next day.

facts.quote: To determine the correct position size from this information, the investor simply needs to divide the account risk ($500) by the trade risk ($20). This means 25 shares can be bought ($500 / $20).
facts.claim: Shares = the dollars you risk divided by the risk per share.

facts.quote: Even with proper position sizing, investors can lose more than their intended risk amount if a security gaps beyond a stop-loss order.
facts.claim: A gap past your stop can cost more than you planned to risk.

facts.quote: Divide your risk per trade by the risk per share, and it'll give you the number of shares to buy
facts.claim: Risk per trade divided by risk per share gives the share count.

facts.quote: The biggest mistake is to decide on your position size first without calculating the space between entry and stop.
facts.claim: Picking the size before measuring entry to stop is the big mistake.

facts.quote: When reported earnings are high relative to expectations, stock prices tend to rise for over 60 trading days. Conversely, when earnings are low, prices continuously fall.
facts.claim: After earnings beat expectations, prices have tended to keep rising for over 60 trading days; after misses, to keep falling.

facts.quote: This post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD), first documented by Ball and Brown (1968) and so named by Bernard and Thomas (1989), is a long-standing robust market anomaly commonly attributed to investor underreaction, among other factors
facts.claim: The drift was first documented in 1968, named in 1989, and is commonly put down to investors underreacting, among other factors.

facts.quote: Several studies, including Chordia, Subrahmanyam and Tong (2014), Milian (2015), and Martineau (2021) argue that PEAD has recently shrunk to the point of disappearance.
facts.claim: Several recent studies argue the classic drift has shrunk to almost nothing.

facts.quote: However, other recent studies, like Ali, Chen, Yao and Yu (2020) and Cox (2020) find that PEAD persists.
facts.claim: Other recent studies find the drift still exists.

facts.quote: The magnitude of PEAD.txt is considerable even in recent years when the classic PEAD is close to zero.
facts.claim: In recent years the classic drift has been close to zero in this paper's sample.

facts.quote: Friday announcements have less immediate and more delayed stock return response.
facts.claim: Friday reports, when attention is low, get less of their reaction at once and more of it later.

facts.quote: They support explanations of post-earning announcement drift based on underreaction to information caused by limited attention.
facts.claim: The findings support the idea that drift comes from investors underreacting because their attention is limited.

facts.quote: Past return and past earnings surprise each predict large drifts in future returns after controlling for the other.
facts.claim: Both a stock's past move and its earnings surprise predicted drift in later returns.

facts.quote: The results suggest a market that responds only gradually to new information.
facts.claim: The market took time to price in new information.

facts.quote: In modern financial markets, stock prices fully reflect earnings surprises on the announcement date, leading to the disappearance of post-earnings announcement drifts (PEAD).
facts.claim: Martineau finds prices now absorb the earnings surprise on report day, so the drift has disappeared.

facts.quote: For large stocks, PEAD have been non-existent since 2006 but has only disappeared recently for microcap stocks.
facts.claim: In his data, large stocks have shown no drift since 2006; microcaps only lost it recently.

facts.quote: A stock that gaps up after reporting strong earnings and closes the day by printing a strong candle (best is a close near highs)
facts.claim: A Power Earnings Gap is a gap up on strong earnings that closes strong, best near the high.

facts.quote: Volume needs to be huge -> at least 3-5x daily average, we want to see other institutions next to us piling into the name
facts.claim: This manager wants gap-day volume at least 3-5x the daily average.

facts.quote: A stock that gaps up on strong earnings only to reverse and close weak or in the red is not what we want to see
facts.claim: An earnings gap that reverses and closes weak or red is not the setup.

facts.quote: Preferably, the stock makes new all-time-highs or 52-week highs and breaks out from at least a month’s range
facts.claim: The best ones make new highs and break out of at least a month-long range.

facts.quote: we suggest leaving the more aggressive trades to very experienced investors, as volatility tends to be very high on these days and stocks can sell-off very sharply.
facts.claim: Earnings gap days are very volatile and can sell off sharply.

facts.quote: Nvidia initially appeared to tamp down the worries about a bubble for AI stocks after reporting a big profit for the summer, along with a forecast for coming revenue that easily cleared analysts' expectations.
facts.claim: Nvidia's report and forecast beat what analysts expected.

facts.quote: Nvidia jumped to an early gain of 5% but then dropped to a loss of 3.2%. Because it's the biggest company in the U.S. market by value
facts.claim: On Nov. 20, 2025 Nvidia rose 5% early, then closed down 3.2%, and it was the biggest US company by value.

facts.quote: The company’s shares declined 3.15% yesterday. And the bloodletting continued for the red-hot semiconductor maker today: Nvidia was down another 3% by midmorning’s trading.
facts.claim: Nvidia closed down 3.15% after its report and was down another 3% by midmorning the next day.

facts.quote: even though Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, delivered blowout, above-expectations earnings.
facts.claim: The drop came even though the earnings beat expectations.

facts.quote: Shares of Nvidia, already one of the world's most valuable companies, skyrocketed Thursday after the chipmaker forecast a huge jump in revenue
facts.claim: Nvidia shot higher on May 25, 2023 after forecasting a huge jump in revenue.

facts.quote: The company based in Santa Clara, California, is close to joining the exclusive club of $1 trillion companies like Alphabet, Apple and Microsoft, after its shares jumped more than 24%.
facts.claim: Nvidia's shares jumped more than 24% that day.

facts.quote: Late Wednesday the maker of graphics chips for gaming and artificial intelligence reported a quarterly profit of more than $2 billion and revenue of $7 billion , both exceeding Wall Street expectations.
facts.claim: The May 2023 report beat Wall Street's expectations for profit and revenue.

facts.quote: The stock has been soaring since its earnings report on May 24 that blew past expectations and positioned the graphics chip company as a leader in the A.I. space.
facts.claim: By May 30, 2023 the stock had kept soaring since the May 24 report.

facts.quote: Nvidia is the latest company whose market capitalization crossed the $1 trillion mark
facts.claim: Within days of the gap, Nvidia's market value crossed $1 trillion.

facts.quote: Default stop: the low of the day, or the prior day's low. (Owner's answer.)
facts.claim: Our default stop is the low of the day or the prior day's low.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: Our stop goes first, a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, and the size comes from it.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: Our stop is the exit: it only moves up, never down or wider, except under our gap rule.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: We buy the full size at one price with one stop, and never add to it.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA.
facts.claim: We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA: too stretched to buy.

facts.quote: 9 and 20 EMA everywhere, with the 50 and 200 SMA.
facts.claim: Our rule: the course teaches the 9 and 20 EMA, with the 50 and 200 SMA.

facts.quote: Stop distance: 1-3% is preferred, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% is acceptable; past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
facts.claim: We like a stop 1-3% away, accept up to 5%, and past 5% we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.

facts.quote: Volume raises the grade; it is not a requirement, except where volume is the setup.
facts.claim: For us volume raises the grade; it isn't a requirement unless volume is the setup.

facts.quote: A strong move may be bought at the trigger right at the open; waiting for the first 30 minutes is the default, not a must.
facts.claim: Our default is to let the first 30 minutes play out; a strong move can be bought at the trigger right at the open.

facts.quote: We buy the full size at one price with one stop: no starter piece, and we never add to a loser.
facts.claim: The full size goes on at one price with one stop: no starter piece, and never an add to a loser.

walkthroughs.title: Where an earnings gap comes from
steps: Say a company reports a strong quarter after the close. Buy orders pile up overnight while the market's shut.
Next morning it opens over yesterday's high. Hold above that high all day and the chart shows an empty space.
That empty space is the gap. Come all the way back to where it was before, and the gap's filled.

walkthroughs.title: Gap and go, or gap and fade
steps: Day one, I watch three things: does it hold the gap, where it closes, and how heavy the volume is.
A close near the high on big volume means buyers kept coming right up to the bell. That's a Power Earnings Gap.
Sell it back under yesterday's close and the gap faded. The buying just wasn't there to hold it.

walkthroughs.title: Risk first, then the drift
steps: Our stop goes under the low of the day or the prior day's low. On a gap up, today's low is closer.
Size from that distance. Gap days swing wide, so you buy fewer shares. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
After a big beat, prices have tended to keep drifting up. People have measured that since 1968.
It's an average, not a promise. Some newer studies say it's shrunk to nothing, at least in big stocks.

questions.q: A stock reports after the close and jumps the next morning. On the daily chart, what has to be true for it to be a real gap up?
choices: Today's low is above yesterday's high
Today's close is above yesterday's close
Today's high is a new 52-week high
Today's volume is well above average
questions.answer: Today's low is above yesterday's high
questions.why: Today's low has to clear yesterday's high. Then nothing traded in between, and the daily chart shows an empty space. That's your gap. An up close alone isn't one, because the two bars can still overlap. A new high or a huge volume bar can come with a gap, but neither one makes it. Why you care: that empty space is the level you watch from here. While price holds above it, the gap is still open.
questions.lesson_line: Look between yesterday's high and today's low. If nothing traded there, you've got a gap.

wrong.Today's close is above yesterday's close: That's just an up day. The two bars can still overlap, so there's no empty space.
wrong.Today's high is a new 52-week high: A new high can happen without any gap at all. It says where price is, not how it got there.
wrong.Today's volume is well above average: Volume tells you how many shares traded, not whether price jumped over a range.

questions.simple: Today's low stays above yesterday's high, so no shares traded in the space between the two bars.

reasons: stable definition, two Tier 2 publishers agree

questions.q: A company beats after the close. Next morning the stock opens well above yesterday's high. What pushed it up there?
choices: Buy orders pile up overnight
The exchange resets the price
Short sellers must cover at open
Thin trading pushes the price up
questions.why: Buy orders piled up overnight. The report hit after the close, so the buying interest built while the regular session was shut. By the open, buyers far outnumber sellers, and price jumps to meet them. After-hours trading is thin, with wide spreads, so that's not what lifts it. The news and the buyers it drew do that. It's also why I treat the regular open as the real test, not the after-hours quote.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings land while the market's shut. Demand piles up, and the open is where you see it.

wrong.The exchange resets the price: Nobody resets it. Price opens higher because buyers outnumber sellers.
wrong.Short sellers must cover at open: Nobody is forced to cover at the open. The gap comes from the news and the demand it built overnight.
wrong.Thin trading pushes the price up: Thin after-hours trading means wide spreads and shaky quotes. The lift comes from the buyers the report drew.

questions.simple: The news hit while the market was shut, so buy orders stacked up overnight and the open jumped to meet them.

reasons: stable mechanism, Tier 1 and Tier 2 facts

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Price trades back to its pre-gap level. The gap has been ___.
questions.why: Filled. A gap is filled when price returns to its pre-gap level. Sources draw the exact line a little differently. Investopedia says the pre-gap level, one StockCharts author the prior close, ChartSchool the last day before the gap. This sentence uses the pre-gap level, so it fits all three.
questions.lesson_line: A filled gap means price went all the way back. The overnight jump is gone.
questions.simple: Filled means price came all the way back to where it was before the gap.

reasons: stable definition; sources differ only on the exact price, handled in the conflicts line

questions.q: An exhaustion gap shows up near the end of a long run, not at the start of one.
questions.why: True. An exhaustion gap comes late, after the stock's already had its big run. It's often the first sign the move is done. The trap is that it looks just like strength: a big gap on big volume. So when I see a huge gap after a long run, I get careful, not excited. Not every late gap is the last one, but that's where the risk sits. Plenty of them fill within a week.
questions.lesson_line: The later a gap comes in a run, the more I respect the chance it's the last one.
questions.simple: True, exhaustion gaps come late in a long run, often right as the move ends.

reasons: stable pattern description, three publishers agree

questions.q: Big beat, and the stock gaps up. A friend says, now watch for the post-earnings drift. What does he mean?
choices: Price keeps going the surprise's way
Price snaps back to prior levels
Volume stays high for weeks after
Estimates creep up before the report
questions.answer: Price keeps going the surprise's way
questions.why: Price keeps going the way of the surprise. That's the drift. After a big beat, prices have tended to keep rising for over 60 trading days. After a miss, they've tended to keep falling. Here's the catch. That's an average across lots of stocks, and several newer studies say it's shrunk to almost nothing. So I treat it as a tailwind at best. It's never a reason to hold a trade that's breaking. Your stop runs the trade, not the drift.
questions.lesson_line: Drift is an average, not a promise. I'll take the tailwind, but my stop runs the trade.

wrong.Price snaps back to prior levels: That's a reversal. The drift research found the move tended to keep going.
wrong.Volume stays high for weeks after: Volume can stay heavy, but the drift is about where price goes.
wrong.Estimates creep up before the report: That's before the report. The drift is what price does after it.

questions.simple: After a surprise, price has tended to keep moving the same way for a while, though newer studies say that's shrunk.

reasons: a research finding that is debated and has shrunk (lesson conflicts line on drift length)

questions.q: Post-earnings drift is mostly blamed on investors underreacting to the news at first.
questions.why: True. The common story is underreaction. People don't take in the whole report on day one, so price catches up over the following days and weeks. Friday reports back that up. Fewer people are watching, so less of the move happens at once and more of it comes later. It's the common explanation, not the only one. What it means for you: day one doesn't always finish the job. That's why a good gap that holds stays on my radar.
questions.lesson_line: Big news can take a while to get priced in. That's why a good gap stays on my radar.
questions.simple: True, the drift is commonly put down to investors reacting too little to the news at first.

reasons: Philadelphia Fed and NBER papers agree

questions.q: A stock is up 15% after hours on its report. What does that tell you about the next open?
choices: The open can be far from that price
It will open exactly 15% higher
The gain is locked in for holders
The open has to be higher still
questions.answer: The open can be far from that price
questions.why: The open can be far from that price. The SEC warns that extended-hours prices may not match the next regular open. Fewer traders, wider quotes.
questions.lesson_line: The after-hours price is a thin first guess. The regular open is the real test.

wrong.It will open exactly 15% higher: After-hours prices may not reflect the next open, the SEC says. It can open well away from it.
wrong.The gain is locked in for holders: Nothing is locked in. By the open the price can be very different.
wrong.The open has to be higher still: It can open higher or lower. The after-hours price is no promise either way.

questions.q: Earnings season. You're hunting for a Power Earnings Gap, an earnings gap worth trading. What do you want to see on day one?
choices: Gap up, heavy volume, strong close
Earnings gap that fills by the close
Small earnings gap on light volume
Gap down that recovers by noon
questions.answer: Gap up, heavy volume, strong close
questions.why: A gap up, heavy volume and a strong close. The close is the big one for me. A close near the high means buyers kept coming all day, not just at the open. Heavy volume means real money is behind it, and we count it as a plus that raises the grade. A gap that reverses and closes weak or red isn't the setup, however good the report was. Check it after the close on day one: the daily candle, with the volume bar under it.
questions.lesson_line: Three things on day one: the gap, the volume behind it, and where it closes.

wrong.Earnings gap that fills by the close: That's a fade. The buyers couldn't hold the gap, and that's exactly what this setup rules out.
wrong.Small earnings gap on light volume: A small gap on light volume shows little conviction. You want a real jump with a crowd behind it.
wrong.Gap down that recovers by noon: Wrong direction. This setup is a gap up on strong earnings.

questions.simple: A gap up on strong earnings, heavy volume, and a close near the day's high.

reasons: a traders' label with no official definition; volume bars differ by author (conflicts line)

deeper.trap: Traders draw the volume line in different places. One manager who trades it wants at least 3-5x the daily average, and Bulkowski wants above the 30-day average. For us volume raises the grade, it isn't a must. Don't let a volume number talk you past what the close is telling you.

questions.q: A stock gaps out of its base on earnings, but volume is light. That gap is more likely to fail than one on heavy volume.
questions.why: True. Light volume on a breakaway gap means fewer buyers showed up, so there's less conviction behind it. Those fail more often and slip back into the old range. Heavy volume shows real demand, and a gap like that may not fill for a long time. For us volume raises the grade, it isn't a must. So I'll still look at one, but as a lower grade, held strictly to its stop.
questions.lesson_line: Volume is the proof behind the gap. Light volume, light conviction.
questions.simple: True, a breakaway gap on light volume is more likely to fail and slip back into the old range.

reasons: the failure claim itself rests on one publisher (Investopedia, unreachable to re-check on 2026-11-12); StockCharts agrees on volume

questions.q: Yesterday's close was $50.00. After earnings it opens at $56.00. How big is the gap, in percent?
questions.why: 12%. Take the open minus yesterday's close and divide by yesterday's close.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap from yesterday's close to today's open. That's the jump the news made.

questions.q: A stock averages 800,000 shares a day. On its earnings gap day it trades 3,200,000. How heavy is that, as a multiple of average?
questions.why: 4x. Divide the day's volume by the average: 3,200,000 over 800,000 is 4. That's four normal days of trading crammed into one session. Real money is showing up, and we count that as a plus that raises the grade. It isn't a pass or fail line, though. Check the close too, because a heavy day that fades is still a fade. You can eyeball it on any daily chart: the gap-day volume bar against the bars before it.
questions.lesson_line: Divide the day's volume by the average. Heavy volume raises the grade, it doesn't make the trade.
questions.simple: 4 times average, because you divide the day's volume by a normal day's volume.

deeper.trap: Average volume can mean a 30-day or a 50-day average, so check which one your chart uses. Authors set different lines too. Bulkowski wants above the 30-day average, and one manager wants 3-5x. Kacher and Morales, as Bulkowski reads them, want at least 1.5 times the 50-day. For us volume raises the grade, it isn't a must.

reasons: computed key

choices: 4x
5x

wrong.0.25x: You flipped it and divided the average by the day's volume.
wrong.40x: Slipped a decimal place. It's 4, not 40.
wrong.5x: One average day too many. 3,200,000 over 800,000 is exactly 4.

questions.q: Yesterday's high was $41.20. Today it opens at $43.00 and dips to a low of $42.10. Is there a gap on the daily chart?
choices: Yes, the low stayed above $41.20
No, it traded below its open
It's filled, it pulled back from $43
Not until volume runs above average
questions.why: Yes, it's a gap. The low of the day, $42.10, stayed above yesterday's high of $41.20. That leaves an empty strip where nothing traded. Dipping under the open doesn't matter. A fill means price gets all the way back to the pre-gap level, and $42.10 never reached $41.20. Volume tells you how much the gap matters, not whether it's there. Mark $41.20 on your chart. While price holds above it, the gap's still open.
questions.lesson_line: Check today's low against yesterday's high. If the low held above, the gap's still open.

wrong.No, it traded below its open: Trading under the open doesn't matter. What counts is the low against yesterday's high.
wrong.It's filled, it pulled back from $43: A fill means getting back to the pre-gap level. $42.10 never reached $41.20.
wrong.Not until volume runs above average: Volume says how much a gap matters, not whether there is one.

questions.simple: Yes, because today's low of $42.10 stayed above yesterday's high of $41.20.

reasons: stable definition applied to given prices

questions.story: A stock gaps up 10% on earnings. Sellers lean on it all day. By the close it's back below yesterday's close.
questions.q: What did the day just tell you?
choices: It faded, the buyers lost the day
Breakaway gap, buy the next open
It still counts as a gap up
Buy it, it's cheaper than the open
questions.answer: It faded, the buyers lost the day
questions.why: It faded, and the buyers lost. A gap that gives it all back the same day is a fade. That 10% jump meant nothing by the bell, because there wasn't enough buying to hold it. That's not the earnings gap we want, whatever the headline said. Buying it there means betting against everyone who just sold the news. I don't buy what the buyers couldn't hold.
questions.lesson_line: A gap that fills the same day is a fade. I don't buy what the buyers couldn't hold.

wrong.Breakaway gap, buy the next open: A breakaway gap breaks price out of a range. This one gave the whole gap back the same day.
wrong.It still counts as a gap up: Not on the daily chart. A gap only stands while price stays above yesterday's high all day.
wrong.Buy it, it's cheaper than the open: Cheaper isn't a reason. The buyers just lost the day.

questions.simple: It faded, because the stock gave back the whole gap the same day, so the buyers couldn't hold it.

reasons: stable definitions, three publishers

questions.story: Two stocks gap up 8% on earnings. The first closes right at the day's high. The second closes near its low, still above yesterday's high.
questions.q: Which one had the buyers in charge all session?
choices: The one that closed at the high
The one near its low, it held the gap
Both, the gaps are the same 8%
Neither, you need volume to tell
questions.answer: The one that closed at the high
questions.why: The one that closed at the high. That close means buyers kept coming right up to the bell, not just a burst at the open that faded. The second one held its gap, so it's still a gap up on the chart. But sellers pushed it down into the close, and they finished in charge. Same 8% gap, completely different day. Volume would add to the picture, but you don't need it here. The close already tells you who won.
questions.lesson_line: Same gap, different day. Where it closes tells me who won.

wrong.The one near its low, it held the gap: Holding the gap keeps it alive, but sellers pushed it down into the close. That's not buyers in charge.
wrong.Both, the gaps are the same 8%: Same gap, different day. Where each one closed tells you who won.
wrong.Neither, you need volume to tell: Volume adds conviction, but the story gives none. The close already tells you who finished in charge.

questions.simple: The one that closed at the high, because buyers kept buying right up to the closing bell.

reasons: two publishers agree on reading the close

questions.q: A stock gaps up on a strong report. The bell rings and it's moving fast. Why might you give it a little time before you buy?
choices: Gaps can fade, let it hold first
Waiting for a fill is a safer entry
The open is usually the day's low
No buys allowed in the first hour
questions.answer: Gaps can fade, let it hold first
questions.why: Gaps can fade, so let it show you it holds. A gap up without enough buying stalls or drops under its open. You don't want to be the one who paid the top of that first pop. Our default is to let the first 30 minutes play out, then buy as price trades through the trigger. It's a default, not a must. A really strong move can be bought at the trigger right at the open. What you don't do is wait for a fill, because on a strong gap that can mean missing the whole move.
questions.lesson_line: Let the gap show me it holds. I'd rather pay a bit more for proof than buy a fade.

wrong.Waiting for a fill is a safer entry: On a strong gap, waiting for a fill can mean missing the whole move. You want proof it holds, not a discount.
wrong.The open is usually the day's low: If it were, you'd just buy the open. A gap without enough buying drops below its opening price.
wrong.No buys allowed in the first hour: There's no such rule. Waiting is our default, and a strong move can be bought right at the open.

questions.simple: Gaps can fade, so giving it a little time shows you whether the buyers can hold it.

reasons: the owner's rulebook C30 (no time-of-day rule) may bear on teaching a wait; see owner_flags

questions.story: You buy an earnings gap on day one at $47.60. The low of the day, LOD for short, is $46.30, about 2.7% under your fill.
questions.q: Where does your stop go?
choices: Just under $46.30, the day's low
Just under $47.60, your entry
Wherever it fits the size you want
No stop, the drift will carry it
questions.why: A few cents under $46.30, the LOD. That's where the chart says you're wrong. It's about 2.7% under your fill, right inside the 1-3% we like. Then the size comes from that stop, never the other way around. A stop just under your entry sounds safer, but earnings days swing hard. A quick dip trips it, and the stock bounces right back without you. Put the stop order in with your broker the moment you're filled.
questions.lesson_line: On the gap day I risk against the low of the day. If it breaks, I'm out.

wrong.Wherever it fits the size you want: That's backwards. The chart sets the stop, and the stop sets the size.
wrong.Just under $47.60, your entry: Earnings days swing hard. A stop right under your fill trips on a quick dip that bounces right back.
wrong.No stop, the drift will carry it: The drift is an average, and it's shrunk. Every trade gets a real stop.

questions.simple: Just under $46.30, the low of the day, because that's where the chart says the trade is wrong.

deeper.trap: A stop under your entry feels safer, but it's the wrong line. Earnings days swing hard, and a quick dip can trigger a stop and bounce right back. If the low of the day sits far below your fill, buy fewer shares or skip the trade. Don't move the stop up to fit a bigger size. Kacher and Morales, as Bulkowski reads them, sell on a close below the gap-day low instead.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (default stop, sizing_rule.md section 2 and A3)

questions.q: Account $40,000, risking 0.5%. You buy the gap at $63.50, stop a few cents under the low of the day at $60.70. How many shares?
questions.why: 71 shares. 0.5% of $40,000 is $200 at risk. $63.50 minus $60.70 is $2.80 a share. 200 over 2.80 is 71.43, so round down to 71. Never round up, or you're risking more than you planned. That stop is about 4.4% away. Wider than the 1-3% I like, but up to 5% I'll take it. Earnings days swing wide, so the stop's far and the share count drops. The dollars at risk stay the same.
questions.lesson_line: A far stop means fewer shares. The dollars at risk stay the same.
questions.simple: 71 shares, because $200 at risk divided by $2.80 a share is 71.43, and you round down.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5: shares from the stop, rounded down)

choices: 72 shares
714 shares
14,285 shares
71 shares

wrong.72 shares: Rounded up. Now you're risking more than the $200 you planned.
wrong.714 shares: Slipped a decimal on the risk. That's 5% of the account, not 0.5%.
wrong.14,285 shares: You divided the whole account by the risk per share and skipped the $200 you're risking.

questions.q: Your stop order sits under the day-one low. It can't fill below that price, even if the stock gaps down next morning.
questions.why: False. A triggered stop becomes a market order. If the stock opens below your stop, the fill can be far worse than the stop price.
questions.lesson_line: A stop limits normal losses. It can't stop a gap. Size so a bad open won't hurt you badly.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A gap that jumps out of a trading range on heavy volume is a ___ gap.
questions.why: Breakaway. A breakaway gap breaks out of a trading range or congestion area, usually on high volume, and can start a new trend. An exhaustion gap is different: it comes near the end of a long trend. A breakaway gap on good volume may not fill for a long time.
questions.lesson_line: Breakaway gaps leave a base behind. Don't count on them filling soon.
questions.simple: Breakaway, because the gap breaks price out of a trading range, usually on heavy volume.

reasons: stable definition, three publishers agree

questions.q: On the day of a big earnings gap, you can already tell whether it's a breakaway gap or an exhaustion gap.
questions.why: False. You only know which kind it was after the stock moves on. An exhaustion gap comes on heavy volume too, so in real time it's easy to mistake for strength. By the time you can name it properly, the move is nearly over. That's why your plan can't wait for the label. You set the stop on day one, under the low of the day. Then the stock tells you which one it was.
questions.lesson_line: You trade the gap before you know its name. That's why the stop goes in on day one.
questions.simple: False, you can only tell the gap's type later, after the stock has moved on.

deeper.trap: Volume will not settle it on the day. Bulkowski says breakaway gaps usually come on high volume, and that exhaustion gaps do too. The same heavy day can turn out to be either one. That is why the plan, and the stop, cannot wait for the label.

reasons: two publishers agree

questions.story: Two stocks gap up on earnings, same size and same volume. The first breaks out of a three-month base near its highs. The second has already doubled in eight weeks.
questions.q: Which gap worries you more as a possible exhaustion gap?
choices: The one that doubled in eight weeks
The base breakout, bases often fail
Neither, size and volume match
The base breakout, it's near highs
questions.answer: The one that doubled in eight weeks
questions.why: The one that doubled in eight weeks. Exhaustion gaps show up late, after a long run, and that stock's had its run. The other one is gapping out of a three-month base. That's where a breakaway gap starts a new trend, and those have done best in a bull market near the yearly high. This is about odds, not a sure call. Either way, you'd still risk against the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Where the gap sits matters. Out of a base, I'm interested. After a double, I'm careful.

wrong.The base breakout, bases often fail: Bases can fail, but that's a failed breakout, not an exhaustion gap. Exhaustion comes after a long run.
wrong.Neither, size and volume match: They match, but they sit in different spots in the trend. Late in a run is where exhaustion gaps show up.
wrong.The base breakout, it's near highs: Near the highs isn't the warning. Breakaway gaps have done best in a bull market near the yearly high.

questions.simple: The one that doubled, because exhaustion gaps tend to come after a long run, not right out of a base.

deeper.counter: A gap out of a base can still fail. A failed breakout gaps above resistance but cannot hold, and falls back into the old range. That is a failed breakaway, not an exhaustion gap, and the stop under the day-one low is what handles it.

reasons: judgment from agreeing pattern descriptions

questions.story: Nvidia, Nov. 20, 2025. The report and the forecast beat expectations. The stock jumps 5% early, then closes down 3.2%.
questions.q: What's that day telling you?
choices: A fade, sellers took the beat
A Power Earnings Gap to buy
Noise, the beat is what counts
Buy the dip, the drift is coming
questions.answer: A fade, sellers took the beat
questions.why: A fade. The numbers were great and the stock was up 5% early. Then sellers took over and it closed down 3.2%. By midmorning the next day it was down another 3%. The report was the news. The close was the market's verdict, and it said no. A Power Earnings Gap needs a strong close, and this day closed red. I'd pass, and I wouldn't argue with it.
questions.lesson_line: The report is the news. The close is the verdict.

wrong.A Power Earnings Gap to buy: That setup wants a strong close. Reversing to close red is exactly what it rules out.
wrong.Noise, the beat is what counts: The beat is the news. The close is the market's answer, and here it was red.
wrong.Buy the dip, the drift is coming: The drift is an average, not a promise. A stock that just reversed on a beat isn't owed one.

questions.simple: It was a fade, because the stock gave back its early gain and closed red despite the beat.

deeper.counter: The 3.2% is AP's figure, and Fortune printed 3.15%. Both tell the same story: a beat that closed red. One red day does not prove the company is weak. It shows buyers did not hold the news that day, and that is what a day-one trade is built on.

reasons: dated news numbers; AP says 3.2% and Fortune 3.15% (conflicts line)

questions.story: Nvidia beat both times. May 25, 2023: up more than 24%, and still soaring into the next week. Nov. 20, 2025: up 5% early, closed down 3.2%.
questions.q: What's the takeaway for the day after a beat?
choices: Trade the reaction, not the headline
Buy the beat, the drift will carry it
Stay out until the earnings news settles
Big names hold up better after beats
questions.answer: Trade the reaction, not the headline
questions.why: Trade the reaction, not the headline. Same company, two beats. In May 2023 the shares jumped more than 24% and kept soaring into the next week. In November 2025 they popped 5% early and closed down 3.2%. The report tells you what happened. What the stock does with it tells you what buyers think. That's the part you trade, and your stop is how you survive the times it goes wrong.
questions.lesson_line: Same company, two beats, two outcomes. I trade what the stock does with the news.

wrong.Stay out until the earnings news settles: That throws out the good ones too. In May 2023 the beat kept soaring into the next week.
wrong.Big names hold up better after beats: Same big name both times. One beat soared, the other closed down 3.2%, so size didn't decide the day.
wrong.Buy the beat, the drift will carry it: The drift is an average, not a promise. In November 2025 a beat closed down 3.2% the same day.

questions.simple: Watch what the stock does after the news, because the same company beat twice and moved two different ways.

deeper.trap: Two good reports can lead to opposite days. The May 2023 report beat on both profit and revenue, and the stock kept running. The November 2025 report also beat, and the stock closed down 3.2%. Buy each on the headline alone, and you get one winner and one red close.

reasons: dated news numbers from two events

questions.q: A buddy says buy the beat and just hold, the drift will carry it. What does newer research say about that drift?
choices: It's shrunk, and studies disagree
It has grown stronger recently
It's now mostly a large-stock effect
It's settled near 60 trading days
questions.why: It's shrunk, and the studies don't even agree on how much is left. Several argue it's shrunk to the point of disappearing. One finds no drift in large stocks since 2006. Others say it still persists. The classic finding, prices rising for over 60 trading days after a beat, came from older data. So buy and hold for the drift isn't a plan. I don't build a trade around it. The chart and your stop come first.
questions.lesson_line: I treat the drift as a maybe, not a plan. The stop and the chart come first.

wrong.It has grown stronger recently: The debate runs the other way. Several studies say it's shrunk to almost nothing.
wrong.It's now mostly a large-stock effect: The reverse. One study finds no drift in large stocks since 2006, and microcaps lost it only recently.
wrong.It's settled near 60 trading days: Over 60 trading days was the old finding. Newer work says it's shrunk, and studies still disagree.

questions.simple: The drift has shrunk, and studies disagree on how much of it is left.

deeper.trap: The classic result, prices rising for over 60 trading days after a beat, describes past averages across many stocks. It is not a holding period for your trade. Newer data says the classic drift is close to zero in recent years.

reasons: research that changes over time; studies disagree (conflicts line)

questions.q: Once a stock prints a strong earnings gap, it will keep drifting higher for months.
questions.why: False. The drift is an average across lots of stocks, not a promise for yours, and newer studies say it's shrunk. One study of good earnings surprises found almost half (48%) rose just 10% and then tumbled, in less than 2 weeks. So a strong gap earns a spot on your radar, not months of blind holding. Have your stop in and your sell plan ready before you count on any drift.
questions.lesson_line: Plan the exit before you count on the drift. Plenty of good gaps give it back fast.
questions.simple: False, the drift is only an average, and in one study almost half of good surprises tumbled within 2 weeks.

deeper.trap: Over 60 trading days is the classic research average, not a forecast for one stock. In Bulkowski's numbers, almost half of good surprises failed inside 2 weeks. Plan the exit before you count on the drift.

reasons: research statistics that can change; drift is debated

questions.story: You bought an earnings gap on day one. Your stop sits a few cents under the day-one low. On day two the stock slides back toward it.
questions.q: It's getting close to your stop. What do you do?
choices: Let the stop work if it's hit
Cancel the stop and wait for drift
Buy more at the lower price
Lower the stop to give it room
questions.answer: Let the stop work if it's hit
questions.why: Let the stop work. You picked that line before you bought, while you were thinking clearly. If price breaks it, the trade's wrong, and you're out with the loss you planned. Don't cancel it, lower it, or buy more. Each one turns a small planned loss into a bigger one. Nobody knows which earnings gap will work, and that's exactly why the stop stays in. If it holds and turns back up, great. Either way the stop makes the call, not your nerves.
questions.lesson_line: When the day-one low breaks, the trade's over. Take the planned loss.

wrong.Cancel the stop and wait for drift: The drift is an average, and it's shrunk. It won't rescue a trade that's breaking.
wrong.Buy more at the lower price: That's adding to a loser, and we never do that. The full size went on at one price, with one stop.
wrong.Lower the stop to give it room: Our stop only moves up, never down or wider. Lower it, and the same shares risk more dollars.

questions.simple: Let the stop work, because you set that line before the trade, and if it breaks the trade is wrong.

deeper.trap: Sliding toward the stop isn't a reason to act early or change the plan. The plan already says where you're wrong. Moving the stop down means the same shares now risk more dollars than you sized for. Hoping for drift doesn't help either: it's an average, and recent studies say it has shrunk. Kacher and Morales, as Bulkowski reads them, sell on a close below the gap-day low instead.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (default stop; A4 the stop never moves down)

questions.story: A stock gaps up on strong earnings and closes near its high on huge volume. At your planned entry it sits 14% above its 9 EMA.
questions.q: What's the play?
choices: Skip it, it's too stretched to buy
Buy it, the close and volume are strong
Buy half now, add on a pullback
Buy it, but set a tighter stop
questions.answer: Skip it, it's too stretched to buy

wrong.Buy half now, add on a pullback: No starter piece. We buy the full size at one price with one stop, and an add is never the plan. This one's too stretched anyway.
wrong.Buy it, but set a tighter stop: Our stop goes a few cents under the low of the day. Squeezing it tighter doesn't fix the stretch.
wrong.Buy it, the close and volume are strong: Strong close, big volume, still 14% above the 9 EMA. Past 10%, we skip it.

questions.simple: Skip it, because it's 14% above its 9 EMA and we skip anything more than 10% above.
questions.why: Skip it. It's 14% above the 9 EMA, and we skip a long that's more than 10% above it. That's too stretched to buy. A strong close and huge volume don't change the distance. That far over the 9 EMA, a stock often needs some time to build out before the next leg. Buy it here and you're the one sitting through that. A tighter stop doesn't fix it, it just puts your stop in the noise. Put it on your radar and let it set up.
questions.lesson_line: A great earnings gap can still be too stretched to buy. Check the 9 EMA first.

deeper.trap: A strong close and heavy volume make a gap feel safe to buy. They say nothing about how far price has run from its 9 EMA. Check that distance first, before the excitement of the day talks you into it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C29 too stretched, A5 no adding, A3 stop)
the 14% is an invented drill number; whether earnings gaps are an exception is flagged for the owner

questions.q: A stock closes at $50.00, then gaps up to open at $56.00 after earnings. At what price is that gap filled?
choices: $50.00, the close
$53.00, halfway back
$56.00, the open
$59.00, further up
questions.why: $50.00, the close. A gap's filled when price comes all the way back to where it was before the jump. This one closed at $50.00 and opened at $56.00, so $50.00 is the line. Back at $53.00, part of the gap is still open. Here's why it matters. When an earnings gap fills, the whole overnight reaction is gone. The buyers who drove it gave it all back, and that tells you a lot about the move.
questions.lesson_line: A gap is filled only when price comes all the way back to where it was before the jump.

wrong.$53.00, halfway back: Halfway back still leaves part of the jump open. It's filled only when price is back at $50.00.
wrong.$56.00, the open: That's where the stock opened. The gap's still wide open there.
wrong.$59.00, further up: A price above the open moves away from $50.00. That widens the gap.

questions.simple: $50.00, because a gap is filled when price comes all the way back to where it was before the gap.

reasons: stable definition: Investopedia, StockCharts and ChartSchool agree

conflicts: What counts as a gap: StockCharts ChartSchool ('Gaps and Gap Analysis') and Bulkowski define an up gap by the day's LOW staying above the prior day's high; StockCharts' 'Gap Trading Strategies' measures from close to open and also counts partial gaps (open above the prior close but not the prior high). q01 and q12 key the low-above-high chart gap and cite both; q10 measures the gap % from close to open and says so in the question. No question asks about partial gaps (only one publisher defines them).

Where a gap is 'filled': Investopedia (Hayes) says the pre-gap level; StockCharts (Bowley) uses the prior close; ChartSchool says a retrace 'at the least, to the last day before the gap'. q03 keys 'filled' for a return to the pre-gap level, which covers all three; no question asks which exact price fills it.

Exhaustion-gap volume: StockCharts ChartSchool, Bulkowski and Investopedia (Mitchell, breakaway-gap page) say exhaustion gaps come on high volume; Investopedia (Hayes, gap-trading page) says 'Low volume should occur in exhaustion gaps.' No question asks about exhaustion-gap volume.

'Gaps 101 tells us that most gaps fill' (StockCharts, Bowley) vs Bulkowski (1% of upward breakaway gaps close within a week; 85% of area gaps do) and ChartSchool ('Avoid falling into the trap...'). Not cited and not asked: the share that fill depends on the type, which is only known later.

Power Earnings Gap: the name is a trader's label (Tramondo credits a trader handle) with no official or academic definition, and the volume bar differs by author: Tramondo 3-5x the daily average, Kacher and Morales 1.5 times the 50-day average (their 'buyable gap-up', as Bulkowski tests it), Bulkowski above the 30-day average. Our own detector (power_earnings_gap.py) uses 8% and 3x, but it is code, not an owner ruling, so it is not used. q08 keys only the three features every source shares (an earnings gap up, heavy volume, a strong close); q11 names each yardstick with its author and keys only the arithmetic.

How long the drift lasts: the Philadelphia Fed paper's classic result is 'over 60 trading days'; Bulkowski's good-earnings-surprise statistics say almost half rise 10% and tumble within 2 weeks; Martineau finds no drift in large stocks since 2006, while Ali et al. (2020) and Cox (2020), as cited by the Philadelphia Fed paper, find it persists. The file never keys a drift length or size for a single stock: it teaches the drift as an average tendency (q05), that it is debated and has shrunk (q24, q25), and never as a reason to hold a broken trade (q16, q26).

Day-one stop: our default (owner's answer, sizing_rule.md section 2) is the low of the day or the prior day's low; Kacher and Morales sell on a CLOSE below the gap-day low; Bulkowski places a stop a few cents below the gap itself (a wider stop). q16 and q26 key our default; q26's story has the price trade through the stop and its reveal says Kacher and Morales use a close. The prior day's low is never a wrong choice.

Nvidia, Nov. 20, 2025: AP (Yahoo Finance copy) says it closed down 3.2% (the Scripps copy of the same story says 3%); Fortune says 3.15%. The file uses AP's 3.2%, which is Fortune's 3.15% rounded. AP says it 'jumped to an early gain of 5%'; no source quoted here gives the opening price, so the file says 'jumped 5% early', not 'gapped up 5%'.

Bulkowski's site asks that it not be used to train AI systems. The file quotes short passages with attribution for teaching people, as it does every other source; the owner may prefer to drop his pages.

'Fade' has two uses. Investopedia (Hayes) calls a gap filled within the same trading day 'fading', and the same page also uses 'fading the gap' for trading against it. This unit uses only the first meaning (w2, q13, q22): a gap up that gives back its gain the same day. It never teaches shorting a gap.
